questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a natural key from a surrogate key?
options: A natural key comes from the source system and may carry business meaning; a surrogate key is generated by the warehouse and is meaningless
A natural key is always an integer; a surrogate key is always text
A surrogate key comes from the source system; a natural key is generated by the warehouse
There is no real difference between the two — they're interchangeable terms
questions.explain: The natural key traces back to where the source system identified the row; the surrogate key is the warehouse's own generated, meaningless identifier.

questions.q: Why does a well-designed dimension table keep the natural key even though the surrogate key is the primary key?
options: For traceability back to the source system, and because the ETL load process uses it for change detection before a surrogate key even exists
SQL Server requires every table to have at least two unique columns
The natural key is actually faster to join on than the surrogate key
Keeping the natural key is optional and has no practical use
questions.explain: You need the natural key to trace a row back to its source, and the ETL process compares incoming rows to existing ones by natural key, since a new row doesn't have a surrogate key yet.

questions.q: What is the accepted exception to the rule that a surrogate key should be meaningless?
options: A date (or time) dimension's surrogate key, conventionally stored as YYYYMMDD (or HHMMSS)
A customer dimension's surrogate key, stored as the customer's name
There is no exception — the rule applies to every dimension without exception
A product dimension's surrogate key, stored as the product's price
questions.explain: Date and time dimensions conventionally use a human-readable, correctly-sorting integer format (YYYYMMDD or HHMMSS) as the surrogate key — the one accepted case where the surrogate key has meaning.

questions.q: In DimDate, which column holds the actual SQL Server DATE data type — the natural key or the surrogate key?
options: The natural key (e.g., FullDateAlternateKey)
The surrogate key (e.g., DateKey)
Neither column uses the DATE data type
Both columns are stored as VARCHAR
questions.explain: The natural key uses the real DATE data type, while the surrogate key (DateKey) is an INT stored in YYYYMMDD format.

questions.q: At design time, how do you decide whether an identifier is a natural key candidate?
options: Ask whether it originates in a source system rather than being invented by the warehouse itself
Check whether the column name contains the word "Key"
Natural keys are always chosen at random
Any column with fewer than 10 characters is automatically a natural key
questions.explain: If an identifier comes from a source system, it's a natural key candidate; the dimension's own primary key should still almost always be a freshly generated surrogate key.
